findings.quote: | Survives the loss of an Availability Zone? | ... | Yes: only One Zone-IA is [not resilient to the loss of availability](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-one-zone-ia-not-resilient) of a zone |
findings.evidence: The linked fact does not say 'only'. Its quote (www/s3/faqs): "However, data in the S3 One Zone-IA storage class is not resilient to the loss of availability or physical loss of an Availability Zone. In contrast, S3 Standard, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 Standard-Infrequent Access, and the S3 Glacier storage classes are designed to withstand loss of availability or the destruction of an Availability Zone." The 'only' is false: fact s3-express-one-zone-single-digit-ms-single-az (docs/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro): "Amazon S3 Express One Zone is a high-performance, single-zone Amazon S3 storage class", and s3-directory-bucket-single-az-express: "you can create a directory bucket in a single AWS Availability Zone". The chapter itself teaches this single-zone class (2-deep 'Go deeper: four bucket types', card s3-c025). Fix: 'Yes: Intelligent-Tiering is [designed to withstand loss of availability] of a zone' with a display from the 'In contrast' sentence; drop 'only'.
findings.resolution: fix-21: the Intelligent-Tiering cell now reads 'Yes, unlike One Zone-IA (not resilient to the loss of availability)'; 'only' is gone. The linked fact s3-faq-one-zone-ia-not-resilient states in its claim that S3 Intelligent-Tiering is designed to withstand the loss of a zone.

findings.quote: 4. **Expire.** At the age you set, S3 deletes the object. ... > **Startup example:** Callvale's rule on callvale-audio moves recordings to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days and deletes them after 7 years.
findings.evidence: callvale-audio is versioned in this chapter's own design (Decision record step 5: 'Versioning keeps earlier versions, and a lifecycle rule moves older recordings to S3 Standard-IA'; diagram s3-after label 'Versioned recordings'; STARTUP.md: 'Amazon S3 (versioning, SSE-KMS, lifecycle rules ...)'). In a versioned bucket an Expiration action does not delete. Fact s3-lifecycle-expiration-versioned-delete-marker, docs/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/intro-lifecycle-rules: "If the current object version is not a delete marker, Amazon S3 adds a delete marker with a unique version ID. This makes the current version noncurrent, and the delete marker the current version." and lifecycle-expire-general-considerations: "Object expiration applies only to an object's current version (it has no impact on noncurrent object versions)." So after 7 years Callvale's recordings (personal data) are still stored and billed (s3-versioning-every-version-billed) unless the rule also has NoncurrentVersionExpiration (fact s3-lifecycle-noncurrent-version-expiration), which the chapter teaches only in quiz question 18. The unlinked step 4 is also a can/does claim without a fact link. Fix: step 4 'In a versioned bucket, expiration [adds a delete marker]; add NoncurrentVersionExpiration to [permanently delete noncurrent versions]', and the startup example 'deletes them after 7 years, and removes the old versions with a noncurrent-version rule'.
findings.resolution: fix-21: lifecycle step 4 now says the object expires, that in a versioned bucket expiration only adds a delete marker (s3-lifecycle-expiration-versioned-delete-marker), and that NoncurrentVersionExpiration can permanently delete noncurrent versions (s3-lifecycle-noncurrent-version-expiration). The startup example now expires the recordings and their old versions after 7 years.

findings.quote: 3. **Your key on each request.** With customer-provided keys (SSE-C), S3 encrypts, but [S3 never stores the encryption key](...). ... | SSE-C | You, in every request | S3 encrypts, but keys stay outside AWS | ... > **Exam signal:** "the company manages its own keys, and the keys are never stored in AWS" points to SSE-C
findings.evidence: Rule broken: RULINGS hard rule 7 ('Where a fact changed since mid-2022, add a "Changed recently" note with old value, new value, date ...'). docs/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ServerSideEncryptionCustomerKeys: "Starting April 2026, SSE-C is disabled by default for all new general purpose buckets and existing buckets in accounts with no SSE-C encrypted objects." and "If your workload requires SSE-C, you must explicitly enable it by setting `BlockedEncryptionTypes` to `NONE` in your bucket's default encryption configuration using the `PutBucketEncryption` API. While SSE-C is blocked, any `PutObject`, `CopyObject`, `PostObject`, Multipart Upload, or replication request that specifies SSE-C encryption is rejected with an HTTP 403 `AccessDenied` error." (also docs/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/default-s3-c-encryption-setting-faq). The chapter recommends SSE-C in five places (1-fast signals row 'AWS must never store the encryption keys', 2-deep table and exam signal, quiz s3-q010 Twin 'SSE-C, because S3 does the work', card s3-c006) and never says that a new bucket rejects it. April 2026 is more than 3 months before the exam, so the change is examinable. Fix: fact request for the April 2026 default, plus a 'Changed recently' note (Old: SSE-C accepted on every bucket; Now: blocked by default on new general purpose buckets; exam: older questions still pick SSE-C for customer-held keys).
findings.resolution: fix-21: new examinable Changed recently entry (2026-04) in 1-fast.md linking s3-sse-c-disabled-by-default-2026-04 (verified); a line in 2-deep encryption step 3 (Starting April 2026, SSE-C is disabled by default on new buckets, so you turn it on first); card s3-c006 extra updated. findings.quote: 3. **Try to delete.** A DELETE with the version ID returns [Access Denied (403 Forbidden)](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-delete-behavior).
findings.evidence: The same fact s3-object-lock-delete-behavior has the other half, which a reader needs: docs/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock: "**Simple `DELETE` request** – If you issued a simple `DELETE` request (a request that doesn't specify a version ID), Amazon S3 returns a `200 OK` response and inserts a delete marker in the bucket, and that marker becomes the current version of the object with a new ID." and object-lock-managing: "Delete markers are not WORM-protected, regardless of any retention period or legal hold in place on the underlying object." With only step 3, a reader expects a locked object to stay visible after any delete; in fact a plain delete 'succeeds' and the object disappears from GET until the marker is removed. findings.resolution: fix-21: presigned step 3 adds 'A page on another domain also needs a CORS configuration on the bucket, to explicitly enable cross-origin requests' (s3-cors-purpose).

findings.quote: **Decision.** Presigned URLs: 15 minutes for an upload, 5 minutes for playback. ... **Trade-off.** A URL works for anyone who holds it until it expires
findings.type: technical: trade-off missing (reasoning from a fact)
findings.evidence: Fact s3-presigned-url-reusable-until-expiry (docs/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url): "Amazon S3 checks the expiration date and time of a signed URL at the time of the HTTP request." findings.quote: A Deny with the condition key [aws:PrincipalOrgID](../facts/s3.md#s3-bucket-policy-deny-outside-org) stops every caller outside your organization.
findings.evidence: AWS service principals do not belong to an organization, so a Deny with StringNotEquals aws:PrincipalOrgID also blocks them, for example CloudFront origin access control, which Callvale adds in chapter 15 (xref in this chapter). full:iam-userguide (section 'Error – Unsupported condition key for service principal'): "you can't use the `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key with the service principal `cloudfront.amazonaws.com`." The S3 guide gives the general rule for Deny statements: "exclude service principals from your `Deny` statements by adding the `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` condition key with a value of `false`" (full:amazons3-userguide, 'Example 6: Requiring a minimum TLS version'). Fix: add 'It also stops AWS services such as CloudFront; exclude them with aws:PrincipalIsAWSService' with a fact.
